frameworks.name: Loss Leader Splinter
frameworks.definition: Itemize all components of your offer, peel off one high-perceived-value component, price it at 80-90% off to drive traffic, then upsell the full bundle at standard margin.

frameworks.name: Gift Card Referral Strategy
frameworks.definition: Sell heavily discounted gift cards (80-90% off face value) limited to 2 per existing customer, restricted to use by friends and family only, capturing referral contact info at point of sale for follow-up and conversion to higher-ticket upsell.

frameworks.name: High-Ticket Scarcity Drop
frameworks.definition: Create a premium offer priced 10-100x the standard offer, limit availability to 5% of your customer base (the top 20% of the top 20% by spend), build advance hype, then publicly count down remaining units to amplify FOMO.

frameworks.name: Buy X Get Y Free (Prepay)
frameworks.definition: Set a differentiated service tier at 2x the standard price, add 1-2 features unavailable in the standard tier to justify the price difference, then offer additional units free (buy 1 get 2, buy 4 get 8) to front-load cash and accelerate customer acquisition.

frameworks.name: MAGIC Offer Wrapper
frameworks.definition: A five-element naming and positioning frame applied to any promotion: Magnetic reason why (M), Avatar specificity (A), Goal/dream outcome (G), time Interval (I), Container word/bucket label (C). Combines to produce an offer name that calls out the right buyer and sets expectation of a specific transformation.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that most businesses generate more revenue in December than in any other single month of the year, driven by two simultaneous forces: businesses advertise at higher volumes and consumers have higher intent to spend.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Advertising volume and consumer spending intent both peak in December, compounding the revenue effect.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a loss leader works because a well-understood commodity product (one whose market price virtually all customers know) brings buyers in the door, where they then purchase ancillary items whose prices are unknown to them and whose margins are substantially higher than the loss leader.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: businesses with multiple product or service components
at least one commodity component with widely known price
claims.mechanism: Customer price-awareness is low for ancillary items; margin on ancillary items exceeds the discount absorbed on the loss leader, producing a net profit gain per transaction.
bounded_by: Requires genuinely ancillary products or services with higher margins than the loss leader; does not work if the entire product line is commodity-priced

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the gift-card referral strategy generates paid new-customer acquisition at a profit: existing customers pay $20 for a $200 face-value gift card (90% off) they give to friends, so the business effectively gets paid to add a referral customer rather than spending marketing dollars to acquire one.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: existing customer base willing to gift services to friends
claims.mechanism: The $20 purchase price offsets the marketing cost of a new-customer acquisition; the referrer pre-sells the new customer, reducing resistance and onboarding friction.

numbers.axis: gift card face value vs. sale price

bounded_by: Gift cards must be restricted to friends and family, not self-use, to generate net-new customers

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that referral customers (those acquired via the gift-card strategy) convert at higher rates and retain at higher rates than cold-acquired customers, because the referring customer pre-frames the relationship and assists with onboarding.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: referral acquisition via existing customer gift cards
claims.mechanism: Referring customer provides social proof and practical onboarding assistance, reducing friction that typically causes early churn.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that limiting the number of gift cards per existing customer (e.g., to two) increases perceived value of the promotion, driving higher purchase rates than an unlimited offer would.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Artificial scarcity per buyer signals that demand exceeds supply, increasing urgency and perceived exclusivity.

numbers.axis: gift cards available per existing customer

anchors.value: 2 units at 70% off = $60 for $400 face value

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that customer spending follows an 80/20 power law, and applying it twice identifies the top 5% of a customer base who will spend approximately 25x more than the median customer, making a 5%-limited high-ticket offer the correct targeting threshold.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any business with a customer base of at least 50+ clients
claims.mechanism: The top 20% of customers spend 5x the median; applying 80/20 a second time within that cohort yields the top 5% of the total base, who are two standard deviations above the mean and willing to spend 10-100x the standard price.

anchors.region: top 5% of customers (20% of the top 20%)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that selling a high-ticket package (priced at 10-50x the standard offer) to only 5% of a 100-person customer base at $5,000 per package generates $25,000, which can double monthly revenue for a business averaging $10,000-$20,000/month from its remaining base.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

numbers.axis: revenue impact of 5% high-ticket upsell on 100-customer base

bounded_by: Assumes all 5 targeted customers convert; actual conversion will vary

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that FOMO-driven public countdown during a scarcity drop (announcing 'four left, three left, two left, sold out') amplifies each subsequent purchase, because each sale announcement functions as social proof that demand is real.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Each sold-unit announcement reduces the perceived supply and validates the offer's value by demonstrating peer buying behavior, triggering FOMO in remaining prospects.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that a 'buy X get Y free' promotion is perceived as significantly more compelling than an equivalent discount, even when the effective discount is identical, because customers anchor on the quantity of free items received rather than the percentage saved.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any product or service business during promotional periods
claims.mechanism: Customers evaluate promotions on the perceived magnitude of the free item relative to the paid item, not on percentage saved; giving more free than paid (buy 1 get 2 free) creates a perception disproportionate to the actual discount.

numbers.axis: perceived vs. actual discount in buy-X-get-Y structures

anchors.region: buy 1 get 2 free (~33% effective unit cost)
buy 1 shirt at $10, get 2 free (3 shirts for $10)
anchors.value: ~30% discount but perceived as far more than 30% off

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that prepaid annual memberships sold at a discount are more financially sound than monthly recurring memberships only when the customer is required to pay the full prepaid amount upfront, with no payment plan permitted at the discounted rate.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service or membership business offering annual prepay at discount
discount rate significant enough to require full upfront payment
claims.mechanism: Allowing a payment plan on a discounted price eliminates the cash-flow advantage and gives the customer price reduction without the liquidity benefit to the business.

numbers.axis: cash-flow comparison: monthly vs. prepaid annual

bounded_by: If business needs consistent monthly cash flow rather than lump sums, prepaid model may create fulfillment mismatch

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that a service-differentiated 'buy X get Y free' promotion can raise the nominal price of the primary offer (e.g., from $100/month to $200/month) without customer objection if 1-2 features unavailable in the standard tier are added, because the upgraded tier is a distinct product with no prior reference price.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: existing business with a defined standard service tier
promotional context where no prior pricing exists for the new tier
claims.mechanism: Absence of a reference price for the new tier eliminates anchoring against the standard price; added features provide rational justification for the price difference so existing customers don't feel disadvantaged.
bounded_by: Does not work if new features are perceived as trivial or already expected by existing customers

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that specifying a named avatar (age, interest, geography, or profession) in a promotional message causes the target audience to self-select and pay attention, whereas generic 'available to everyone' messaging is ignored because it signals low relevance.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Specificity signals relevance; a named avatar triggers pattern recognition in the matching reader ('this is for me'), lifting attention and conversion versus broad undifferentiated messaging.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that Best Buy gift cards have an unusually low redemption rate, meaning a significant share of purchased gift cards are never redeemed, turning them into interest-bearing, eventually forgiven loans from customers to the business.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Gift card float earns interest on the business's balance sheet; upon expiration, unredeemed balances convert to pure profit with no goods delivered.
bounded_by: Specific redemption rate not quantified in transcript; varies by retailer and gift card type

examples.text: Alex Hormozi uses diapers as the canonical loss leader example: diapers.com (a real company) sold diapers below market price because virtually all parents buying from a baby-product store know the going rate for diapers, making price comparison trivial. The strategy worked because ancillary items (non-drip baby bottles, accessories) had opaque pricing and high margins. According to Hormozi, diapers.com used this approach to capture market share in the baby category, recouping the diaper discount many times over through high-margin accessory purchases.

Alex Hormozi describes a Nashville boot store he observed that had been operating for 10+ years and had expanded, suggesting sustained profitability. The entire front window read 'Buy one, get two free.' Inside, boots were priced at $600 a pair when typical cowboy boots retail around $200. The store had simply tripled the unit price of one pair, then offered two additional pairs free, targeting bachelorette parties where groups of women would pool the free pairs among friends. The effective per-pair cost was $200, unchanged from the market rate, but the promotion drove group buying behavior and high unit volume per transaction.

Alex Hormozi illustrates the gift-card strategy using a gym scenario: a gym owner sells $200 face-value gift cards (equal to one month's membership) to existing members for $20 each (90% off), capped at two per member, and restricted to gifts for friends and family. When a new customer receives the $200 gift card, they don't know the purchase price was $20. The gym owner collects cash immediately (paid customer acquisition), the existing member earns social credit for giving a generous gift, and the new customer arrives pre-warmed by their friend. The gym then seats each new customer in a sales consultation to upsell a $1,000 program, converting the $200 gift card into an $800 net additional sale.

Alex Hormozi provides a 'busy moms' spa example to demonstrate the MAGIC wrapper in action: M = holidays (magnetic reason why: Black Friday season), A = busy moms (avatar), G = relaxation (goal), I = 30 days (interval), C = getaway (container word). The resulting offer name is 'Busy Mom's 30-Day Relaxation Getaway for the Holidays.' This name can be applied to any of the four underlying promotional mechanics (loss leader, gift card, high-ticket, or buy X get Y free) to make the offer feel purpose-built for a specific person rather than a generic promotion.

practices.text: To implement the loss leader strategy: itemize every component of your offer (e.g., facility access, accountability, workouts, nutrition guides), select one component to promote at 80-90% off, market that single component aggressively, then upsell the full bundle once the prospect engages.

When executing the gift card referral strategy, collect the contact information of the recipient at the point of gift card sale, then use it to send a three-way introduction between the existing customer and the new prospect, enabling follow-up if the gift card is never redeemed.

For high-ticket scarcity drops, build advance hype before the launch date, announce the exact time the offer goes live, instruct prospects to have credit cards ready, then publicly announce remaining unit counts after each sale to sustain FOMO momentum.

When launching a new facility or service and using the prepay buy X get Y free promotion, limit the promotion to the first 50 or 100 buyers to de-risk fulfillment and capture immediate cash to cover opening costs without drawing on reserves.

Apply the MAGIC wrapper to every holiday promotion by naming the avatar explicitly, stating the dream outcome and the time interval, and using a container word (blueprint, accelerator, program, intensive, launchpad, getaway) to bucket all offer components into a single branded product name.

For recurring membership businesses using prepay promotions, require full upfront payment at the discounted price and do not offer a payment plan; the entire business rationale of the prepay discount is cash collected immediately.
